newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Russia says fears Taleban, will defend interests.
newsitem.headline: Russia says fears Taleban, will defend interests.

text.p: A senior Russian military official said on Saturday that Moscow was worried by the spread of militant Islam from Afghanistan and made it clear it would continue to defend its strategic interests in Tajikistan.
General Andrei Nikolayev, who commands Russia's Border Guard Service, chaired a military council of Russian frontier troops, who defend the former Soviet state's border with Afghanistan.

Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, whom Moscow backed in a four-year civil war against the Islamist rebels with whom he recently signed a peace deal, told the meeting a million Afghans could flee the Taleban across the mountain frontier.
After four hour of talks in the Tajik capital, Dushanbe, Nikolayev told a news briefing that the progress of the purist Islamic Taleban movement in Afghanistan had been the main issue.
"This situation worries the leadership of Russia and the Central Asian states," Nikolayev said.
The Taleban militia has installed strict Sharia law in Afghanistan and controls most of its territory, except for the north, bordering Tajikistan.

Russia and the five former Soviet states in Central Asia are worried that a wave of radical Islam and instability may spread across their frontiers if the Taleban mount a successful summer campaign against the forces of General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Ahmad Shah Masood, who now control northern Afghanistan.

Around 20,000 Russian peacekeepers and border guards are deployed in Tajikistan. Russia, which is separated from Tajikistan by more than 1,000 km (700 miles) of Kazakh territory, sees them as a buffer against the spread of militant Islam.

Asked what was Russia's mission in Tajikistan, Nikolayev said: "Russia is not only a European state but an Asian one as well...To numerous questions about what Russia is doing in Tajikistan, we answer that Russia is defending its interests."
Nikolayev said around 100,000 refugees were ready to flee immediately from northern Afghanistan to Tajikistan in the case of an escalation of fighting there.
Addressing the council earlier, Rakhmonov said more than a million refugees could pour into Tajikistan.
Another issue which appeared to have been discussed was that of drug trafficking from Afghanistan.
Nikolayev said a whole industry was already producing drugs in Afghanistan. Russian border guards seized several tonnes of opium last year and large amounts of heroin.
He said that two units of Russia's 201st infantry division were currently helping safeguard the border. Nikolayev gave no further details about the secretive council.

Kazakhstan sent a representative but the other former Soviet Central Asian -- Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan -- declined to take part in the council, which Moscow had hoped would work out a joint strategy against threats to stability.
A Russian military source told Reuters that police on Saturday found the body of a serviceman from the 201st division murdered in Dushanbe several days earlier.

Uncontrollable armed bands -- including those operating from bases in Afghanistan -- often disturb the ceasefire between Tajikistan's secular government and the Islamist opposition agreed last year to end the war which killed tens of thousands.
